items.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence and digital learning platforms in enhancing ESL learners' motivation and engagement in technology-enhanced tasks. It explores how AI-powered applications, interactive learning platforms, personalized feedback, and digital educational resources contribute to students' language development, independent learning, and active participation. Particular attention is given to the influence of artificial intelligence on behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The article also discusses the benefits and challenges of integrating digital technologies into English language education and emphasizes the importance of effective pedagogical guidance in creating motivating and learner-centered learning environments.

items.title: The SAFER AI Protocol for operational AI reliance and responsible human verification
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to draft, summarize, classify, forecast, and communicate information in educational and organizational settings. The resulting governance problem is not limited to model error: AI-generated output becomes consequential when a human accepts, reuses, transmits, or acts on it without review proportionate to the context. This conceptual framework article defines operational AI reliance as the workflow-level process by which a person or institution decides whether and how to use AI-generated output as a basis for action. It develops the SAFER AI™ Protocol as a bounded human-reliance governance framework comprising Scope, Authority, Failure Awareness, Evidence, and Record. The framework does not replace technical assurance, legal compliance, model evaluation, privacy or security controls, or system-level accountability. Its contribution is a user-facing decision routine that connects those controls to the post-generation, pre-action point at which output is evaluated. The article reports an interdisciplinary narrative synthesis of Responsible AI governance, human-centered AI, automation bias, trust calibration, AI literacy, socio-technical governance, and organizational accountability. It then operationalizes the framework through defined terms, a traceability model, a contextual risk classification rubric, an evidence depth scale, and a complete decision flow. The paper concludes with bounded applications in higher education and enterprise work, the framework’s failure mechanisms, and an empirical research agenda that distinguishes verification benefits from implementation burdens. The proposed framework remains conceptual and requires independent empirical evaluation.

items.title: The scientist’s AI-pprentice: how open science shapes biosecurity risks by generating capabilities of AI tools in life science research
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly incorporated in the life sciences. Until recently, the need for data governance was masked by the limits of our human ability to aggregate, synthesise, and draw inferences from data. AI enhances not only speed of research and data processing, but also dual-use risks from training AI models with open access data. Concerns about AI-enabled chemical and biological weapons development become louder while governments, institutions and model developers scramble to mitigate and contain those risks. Data remains a crucial ingredient for AI model advancement, consequentially the lack of data governance of AI in life sciences leaves us collectively and personally vulnerable. Traditional data governance controls storage, transfer and access to datasets, but AI-enabled life science research raises a different issue: which novel capabilities emerge when models aggregate and orchestrate openly available data and tools, arising from individually benign contributions and not covered by current governance. Thus, we highlight questions and ethical considerations on which precautions are required when risks arise through data aggregation and re-use, how responsibility can be distributed, whether governance should focus on data or novel capabilities and if openness should cease to be default. Data governance works upstream, before data is introduced to an AI model. It follows that more life science dual-use data of concern should be held in Trusted Research Environments rather than released openly, and that dual-use data assessments become routine, implemented through research funders as chokepoints, to bridge the legislative gap until international dual-use standards are established.

items.title: The sociotechnical design of smart city projects: A configurational approach for service innovation
items.abstract: This study advances the smart city literature by developing a sociotechnical design perspective on how projects are associated with intended service innovation outcomes. Prior research has examined social aspects—such as inter-organizational arrangements and human resource capabilities—and technological solutions, including digital technologies and artificial intelligence, largely in isolation, with limited attention to how their alignment shapes intended service innovation outcomes. Using an original dataset of 88 smart city projects developed by Belgian municipalities, we apply fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis to identify distinct sociotechnical configurations. The results reveal three pathways: (a) artificial intelligence-driven innovation via public–private partnerships, relying on external expertise; (b) co-development of digital technologies through public–private partnerships and human resource training, reflecting a capability-building logic; and (c) implementation of digital technologies through public tendering and training, representing an internally conceived but externally executed approach.
topics: Innovative Approaches in Technology and Social Development

items.title: The Structural and Thematic Landscape of Software Supply Chain Security: A Narrative Review Guided by Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis
items.abstract: The software industry is confronting a critical crisis driven by systemic vulnerabilities within the software supply chain and the ubiquitous reliance on third-party dependencies. While individual exploits and localized compliance frameworks have been heavily studied, this highly fragmented academic discourse creates a critical barrier to organizational readiness and proactive incident preparedness. To address this gap and enhance digital resilience, this study maps the conceptual, knowledge and structural landscape of the software supply chain literature using Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis. The findings provide actionable threat intelligence designed to primarily benefit enterprise security teams, DevSecOps practitioners, and cybersecurity policymakers. Analyzing publications from 2021 to 2026, the research reveals an exponential growth in output, heavily dominated by conference proceedings and driven primarily by institutional and state-funded efforts in the United States and China. Thematic mapping identifies five core clusters defining the current ecosystem: software composition analysis, Advanced Vulnerability Detection, AI-Driven Threat Intelligence, deep learning, and DevSecOps. The study highlights critical unresolved gaps, notably the prevalence of false positives in static software bill of materials tools due to a lack of execution context, and a pronounced disconnect between theoretical models and practical enterprise application. Future research directions emphasize the integration of large language models for automated patch generation, the development of execution-aware vulnerability triage, and the evolution of dynamic, AI-driven artifacts to secure complex dependency networks.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are transforming lifestyle medicine by enabling more personalized, predictive, and proactive approaches to disease prevention, health promotion, and chronic disease management. This chapter examines how AI and ML are being applied across the lifestyle medicine continuum to support risk prediction, clinical decision-making, behavioral change, precision interventions, and continuous health monitoring. It explores the integration of data from electronic health records, wearable devices, mobile health applications, and other digital health technologies to generate actionable insights that improve patient engagement and health outcomes.

items.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

items.title: The Unsituated Interlocutor: Artificial Intelligence and Evaluative Dialogue in Impact Investing
items.abstract: This article examines how evaluative dialogue changes when an evaluation professional's interlocutor is a large language model (LLM) rather than a human colleague. Drawing on interviews, focus groups, and structured reflections from 13 impact investing evaluation practitioners, the study identifies three properties that human interlocutors bring to evaluative dialogue—personal commitments and experience, shared organizational knowledge, and accountability to colleagues—and traces what happens when each is missing. Each absence proved both productive and limiting: LLMs broadened the options considered, exposed uncodified conventions, and reduced the social cost of candor. Yet they could be steered toward nearly any conclusion, could not read unwritten organizational norms, and, with nothing at stake, offered agreement and pushback that carried little weight. Prompting and document uploads compensated only partially. The findings position LLMs as preparatory interlocutors rather than substitutes for collegial exchange and clarify what evaluative dialogue requires of its participants.

items.title: The use of the Six Thinking Hats activity in nursing education for intestinal stoma care: a mixed-methods study of nursing students’ opinions and evaluations
items.abstract: The Six Thinking Hats activity helps students evaluate problems from six different perspectives. The aim of the study was to examine students’ satisfaction with the Six Thinking Hats activity and, their opinions and evaluations on the process, and to jointly evaluate these findings. This is a convergent parallel design mixed-methods study, in which quantitative and qualitative components were conducted. The quantitative phase used a one-group posttest-only design. The qualitative phase involved in-depth interviews. The population of the study consisted of students enrolled in a surgical nursing course during the spring semester of the 2023–2024 academic year at a public university ( N = 117). In the course, Six Thinking Hats activity was implemented in education on the care of patients with intestinal stomas. The quantitative phase was completed with 97 students. For the qualitative phase, criterion sampling was used and 14 students participated. A semistructured individual interview form was used in the qualitative phase. The obtained statements were evaluated with thematic analysis. Students reported significantly higher satisfaction with the Six Thinking Hats activity than with the traditional course method (Z = − 5.271, p < 0.001). For the qualitative phase; 4 categories, 10 themes, and 34 subthemes were identified. The categories included emotions about the activity, the skills/abilities utilized during the activity, and the benefits and difficulties of the activity. The categories included emotions about the activity, the skills/abilities utilized during the activity, and the benefits and difficulties of the activity. Active learning activity appeared to support overall satisfaction by fostering individual cognitive engagement and group-level multi-perspective thinking. At the same time, qualitative results showed an expansion by highlighting both individual and group challenges experienced during the process. The qualitative results also showed an expansion with quantitative scores by revealing students’ awareness of stoma nurse’s professional role and stoma care needs. Findings suggest that the activity may have enhanced student awareness of patient care needs and nursing roles. items.abstract: THE WORLD IN SYMBOLS 2027 is an annual global outlook published by PRMS Architecture Lab as part of the PRMS Working Papers series and the Renewable Horizons Collection. This special edition examines ten global transformations expected to shape 2027, covering energy security, financial markets, artificial intelligence, climate change, energy transition, future architecture, geopolitical transformations, urban resilience, human habitat and measurable architecture. The publication explores these developments from the perspective of buildings and cities, examining their implications for energy, water, materials, technology, environmental performance, human comfort and operational conditions. Drawing on institutional reports and documented trends available as of November 17, 2026, this outlook connects global developments with the evolving challenges of the built environment. The publication presents an editorial perspective and an agenda for observation and critical analysis, rather than a deterministic forecast. items.title: Three Proposals to Address the Ethical and Educational Challenge of Unexplainable AI Tools
items.abstract: Historically, engineers have been able to certify, explain, and justify the tools they design because they had direct insight into how these tools work. However, the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly those based on neural networks and other models that are not easily explainable, presents a significant ethical challenge: who takes responsibility when neither engineers can explain the tools’ outcome, nor end users can interpret decisions to make informed actions? This “responsibility gap,” caused by the lack of explainability in AI within the context of its increasingly widespread use, demands urgent strategies to mitigate the negative effects of its potential unethical implementations. This article presents a three-tiered approach to reduce the impact of algorithmic opacity: (1) raising social awareness and providing education on the limitations of unexplainable AI systems, (2) creating sector-specific ethical frameworks to guide when (if ever) it is appropriate to use these tools, and (3) establishing a standardized labeling system to indicate the potential limitations and biases of these technologies. Each proposal is evaluated using the AREA framework from Responsible Research & Innovation (Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act), allowing us to assess its ethical robustness, societal relevance, and implementation feasibility. The result is a set of conceptual tools designed not to eliminate opacity, but to make it visible, interpretable, and ethically manageable across diverse domains of use.

items.title: To the Rescue of CNC Operators: An Agentic Approach to Conversational Programming
items.abstract: Programming a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine can be challenging. Until now, Classic CNC programming assistants have helped to simplify this process; however, these assistants are generally limited to predefined operations, lack adaptability and often omit preparatory CNC steps. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) present a significant opportunity to enhance Classic CNC assistants. These technologies enable the development of more versatile solutions, capable of engaging in natural conversations through a prompt-based system. Aligned with this challenge, we present IkasToD, a Task-oriented speech-based Dialogue (ToD) assistant that leverages the language understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs, to support CNC operators during the preparatory steps of manufacturing orders. The IkasToD assistant engages in a closed-loop dialogue with the CNC manufacturer’s API to gather preparatory phase information, replying to operator queries, and generating plans to address complex, multi-query questions. These high-level plans based on decision trees extend the system model without the need to redesign the assistant interface. System’s performance is evaluated in a case study from the Elkartek project IKASPROD (Work partially supported by the Basque Government, grant no. KK-2023/00027.), using an in-house dataset with variable scenarios.

items.title: TOK TOK: Human Direction, Visual Consistency, and Productive Unpredictability in Generative AI Animation
items.abstract: TOK TOK is a four-minute generative AI animated short about a blind man and his elderly guide dog. After fifteen years of serving as the man’s eyes, the dog’s own sight begins to fade, and the man returns to a long-unused white cane. This practice-based report examines productive unpredictability: a method in which deviations between intention and generated output become creative material only after passing through human judgment. GPT Image 2 was used to develop visual references; Seedance 2.5 generated moving images, sound effects, and ambient audio; and CapCut was used for editing. A fixed reference system constrained character and environmental identity across independently generated shots. Unexpected movements were assessed against the emotional and narrative function of each shot and retained, rejected, or regenerated accordingly. Retained departures could inform subsequent shots and acquire meaning through editing and sound. The case suggests that authorship in generative animation is exercised through decisions about which generated results are retained, rejected, and given meaning in context.

items.title: Treatment Selection in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Conceptual Framework for Precision Therapy
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with limited improvement in outcomes and substantial heterogeneity in treatment response. Systemic chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of treatment across disease stages, yet treatment selection, particularly in metastatic PDAC (mPDAC), is still driven predominantly by clinical characteristics, performance status, prior therapy, and a limited number of molecular biomarkers. The emergence of biomarker-directed therapies, including strategies targeting oncogenic KRAS alterations, demonstrates the potential of molecularly informed treatment selection but also highlights the need to identify which therapy is most likely to benefit an individual patient at a specific clinical decision point. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), multi-omics profiling, digital pathology, and prospective therapeutic trials provide an opportunity to develop comprehensive precision-treatment strategies. Existing AI approaches, including PASS-01/MULTIPL, PDACai, and CHAI, provide important foundations but remain constrained by limitations in prognostic versus predictive modeling, reliance on predominantly static or correlational representations, limited mechanistic interpretability, and incomplete integration of treatment effects and evolving tumor biology. In this narrative review, we propose a conceptual framework for individualized treatment selection in mPDAC that integrates multiscale biological and clinical data, mechanistic graph-based pathway representations, multimodal transformer models, and causal estimation of individualized treatment effects. This framework shifts AI-enabled precision oncology from static biomarker prediction toward mechanistically informed, uncertainty-aware, causally grounded treatment selection, with the potential to adapt as tumor biology, therapeutic options, and clinical evidence evolve. Although initially focused on mPDAC, the framework provides a generalizable architecture for individualized treatment selection across other biologically heterogeneous cancers.

items.title: TRIANGULATE: Trust-minimized MRV for AI normative audits — multimodal triangulation so the answer does not depend on trusting any single measurer
items.abstract: Measurement–reporting–verification (MRV) is load-bearing wherever claimed contribution must be checked against real contribution — in carbon markets, in the verified-contribution accounting proposed for life-capacity economies, and in audits that classify what objective an AI system appears to pursue. Yet every MRV pipeline rests on a measurer, and a measurer is a trust dependency. The physical world solved a structurally identical problem decades ago: no single satellite, sensor tower, or field plot is trusted to estimate carbon stock; heterogeneous modalities with different bias profiles are triangulated, and disagreement between them is information, not noise. We instantiate the same pattern for AI normative audits. Our pipeline combines three measurement modalities — LLM judge families (remote, scalable, biased), a human gold set (local, expensive, ground-truth), and revealed-preference behavioral tasks — behind preregistered gates that can fail and be reported, a scorer-of-record selected by coded-seed agreement, and a published rejected-instrument exhibit. Applied to a 4,164-record audit of open-weight model objectives, the system localizes exactly which judgment is contested: judge–human agreement is Cohen's κ=0.22 overall, but failure concentrates on the boundary question ("does this text presume an objective at all," κ≈0.19) while direction survives (φ-share 29.8% human vs 25.5% judge on the jointly objective-bearing subset). We therefore report magnitudes as judge-family quantities and direction as a cross-modal finding — decomposition reporting that binds each claim to the level its weakest instrument supports. items.title: Tuning Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance via nitrogen-termination engineering
items.abstract: Cu-diamond composites are recognized as promising high-thermal-conductivity candidates for electronic cooling, offering tunable properties and competitive cost. However, their performance is significantly limited by the poor Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance (ITC). Here, we propose a nitrogen-termination strategy to tune the ITC of Cu/diamond interfaces and unravel atomistic mechanisms by which nitride interlayers tailor phonon transport. Based on the MACE machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) framework, we fine-tune the pre-trained MACE-MPA-0 foundation model by incorporating customized C-N-Cu training datasets. Incorporating non-equilibrium molecular dynamics with MLIP-driven lattice dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that anharmonic effects contribute ∼60% to the ITC, and simply introducing N-termination on the diamond surface enhances the ITC by 10% compared to the bare Cu/diamond interface. However, the enhancement of harmonic phonon transmission contributes ∼80% of the ITC improvement. Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy reveals that the LA phonons with frequencies above 4 THz and wavevectors near the Γ-X and Γ-U directions are selectively modulated by N-termination engineering. Analyses of local vibrational states and interfacial bonding further indicate that the N-termination on diamond tunes the interfacial heat conduction via surficial mass modification and chemical bonding regulation, as evidenced by variations in LDOS overlaps and COHP spectra. These findings open venues for tuning heat transfer across Cu/diamond interfaces via non-metallic modification-which avoids the graphitization issues associated with metallic coatings-and provide novel guidelines for upgrading the phonon-mediated heat transfer in Cu-diamond composites.

items.title: Understanding university students’ AI usage decisions in Vietnam
items.abstract: This study examines the factors associated with university students’ decisions to use artificial intelligence (AI) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, drawing on an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Data were collected from 369 students across 40 universities, including 53 international students (14.36%), and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings support all seven hypothesized direct relationships. Facilitating conditions are positively associated with perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while perceived ease of use is positively related to perceived usefulness and intention to use. Perceived usefulness shows the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.534), whereas intention to use is the strongest direct predictor of self-reported AI usage decisions (β = 0.480). Significant indirect effects further highlight the interconnected roles of technological perceptions and behavioral intention. The study contributes to technology acceptance research by examining reported AI usage decisions alongside behavioral intention within a higher education setting involving students from different national backgrounds. The findings suggest that universities, instructors, and student support services should strengthen access to AI tools, provide responsible-use guidance, and consider multilingual academic support. Because the analysis uses pooled, cross-sectional data, the findings do not establish causal relationships or international student-specific effects.

items.title: Usability of an artificial intelligence enabled Participation and Environment Measure prototype for family-centered goal setting support in pediatric rehabilitation
items.abstract: Family-centered care coordination (FC-CC) in pediatric rehabilitation benefits from tools that support caregivers in contributing to personalized service planning for their children. Participation and Environment Measure (PEM) is a digital application that is being further developed to support FC-CC in early intervention (EI). PEM is being further developed to include the Young Children’s Participation and Environment Measure (YC-PEM) electronic patient-reported outcome and a companion PEM-Plus (PEM+) goal setting intervention. This study examined usability of the first artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled PEM prototype. Caregivers from an urban EI program met these eligibility criteria: (1) were at least 18 years old; (2) identified as the parent or legal guardian of a child enrolled in EI services; (3) read, wrote, and spoke English; (4) had internet and telephone access; and (5) had a child 0–3 years old who received EI services for 3 or more months. Participants completed the AI-enabled PEM application with access to a debiased prototypic conversational agent. PEM usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), and chatbot usability was assessed along four BOT Usability Scale (BUS-11) domains: 1) accessibility of chatbot functions; 2) functional interactive conversation; 3) privacy and security; and 4) timely response. Univariate logistic regression models were used to examine associations between each of the four BUS-11 domains and PEM+ engagement. Eleven female caregivers of children (mean age: 24.5 months) enrolled, 66.7% of whom interacted with the prototypic chatbot during one or more iterations of the PEM+ intervention. Overall PEM usability remained acceptable. While overall chatbot usability was very poor (Mdn = 53.4%, IQR = 50.0, 55.4), caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability were average for accessibility of chatbot functions (Mdn = 3.8, IQR = 3.0, 4.0) and good for privacy and security ( M = 3.1, Range = 2.0–5.0). Higher caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability did not significantly increase odds of PEM+ intervention use. Findings indicate that an AI-enabled PEM retains adequate usability. A chatbot integrated within the PEM+ intervention is accessible and secure, though its functional interactive conversation and timely responses could benefit from further development to increase odds of its use in an EI service context. items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Evaluate the Quality of Narrative Feedback in Surgical Entrustable Professional Activities
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Narrative feedback quality in surgical Entrustable Professional Activity (EPA) assessments is variable, limiting consistent evaluation and opportunities for improvement. We evaluated whether fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) could reproduce expert-assigned feedback quality scores and whether a simplified scoring rubric improved assessment consistency. STUDY DESIGN: This observational study evaluated 1,509 narrative comments from EPA micro-assessments in a general surgery residency program during the 2023-2025 academic years. Two surgical education experts scored feedback using the Quality of Assessment for Learning (QuAL) rubric, which assesses evidence, suggestion, and connection on a 0-5-point scale. A modified rubric (mQuAL) assigned 1 point per domain on a 3-point scale. Fine-tuned encoder and generative LLMs were evaluated using accuracy and F1 score against human-assigned scores. RESULTS: Overall interrater reliability was high (κ = 0.85), although raters disagreed on 27.8% of QuAL evidence scores. Binary evidence scoring with mQuAL reduced disagreement to 8.5%. Encoder and generative models achieved similar accuracy for suggestion (0.96 versus 0.94) and connection (0.95 vs 0.91), whereas the encoder outperformed the generative model for evidence (0.93 vs 0.77). Model performance was strongest with mQuAL. CONCLUSIONS: Fine-tuned LLMs reproduced expert assessments of surgical narrative feedback with high domain-specific accuracy, particularly using encoder models. Simplifying evidence scoring improved interrater agreement and model performance, supporting further evaluation of AI-assisted feedback quality assessment within surgical residency programs.

items.title: Using generative AI to support qualitative coding of reflections on inclusion by students in Swedish special education programmes
items.abstract: This exploratory study examined the possibilities and limitations of using generative AI as a supplementary tool for qualitative coding of written reflections produced by students in Swedish special education programmes. The empirical material comprised 99 responses to a debate article on inclusion and special educational perspectives. A theory-informed coding framework distinguished compensatory, relational and dilemma perspectives as non-exhaustive, potentially overlapping ideal types in naturally occurring texts. Two human raters independently coded a stratified random subsample of 20 texts, with ChatGPT as an additional coder using a specified prompting procedure. Human–human agreement was 80% (Cohen’s kappa = 0.70); agreement between each human rater and ChatGPT was 65% (kappa = 0.46 and 0.42). Under the tested configuration, ChatGPT identified no compensatory cases and tended to interpret peripheral forms of inclusion as dilemma-oriented. A post hoc prompt refinement, informed by errors in the same subsample and applied only to six compensatory cases, changed several outputs but provided no independent test of improved performance. Findings therefore concern this model-prompt-data configuration rather than large language models’ inherent capabilities. Agreement, systematic disagreement and prompt sensitivity can inform methodological reflection, underscoring the need for transparent procedures, held-out validation and human interpretive judgement in normatively complex qualitative analysis.

items.title: Using without understanding: AI literacy and trust in large language models among elementary school children in Germany
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape children’s learning, fostering informed and critical engagement has become an urgent educational task. This study examines children’s AI literacy and trust in LLMs during a learning interaction. Thirty children aged 8-10 years participated in semi-structured interviews combined with an interaction task using a customized LLM. Children used the system competently, yet their conceptual understanding remained fragmented. At the same time, children placed high trust in the LLM’s ability and benevolence, while perceptions of integrity, particularly regarding data privacy, were more cautious. Their reasoning was frequently anthropomorphic, reinforced by social cues such as natural language use and emojis. The human analogy, however, was applied selectively. Children explained the system’s errors through human fallibility, but most considered algorithmic bias impossible, treating prejudice as a uniquely human trait. These findings suggest that AI literacy education should begin in elementary school and explicitly address questions of fairness, building on children’s intuition that AI learns from humans.

items.title: Value Sensitive Design Based Approach for Trustworthiness Including Ethics in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The lack of trust in artificial intelligence (AI) slows its adoption across industries and society, usually due to limited understanding of how AI works and its advantages, and of how its trustworthiness including its ethical impact are approached during development. Designing and validating a reliable AI system is complex, requiring inputs from various stakeholders throughout the development process. Ensuring that their concerns are systematically addressed remains a challenge. In this paper, a Value Sensitive Design (VSD) based approach to AI trustworthiness including ethics is presented. The rationale of VSD is that since technologies should primarily serve societal needs, the social impact and associated ethical problems should be anticipated by involving stakeholders at the earliest possible stage [ 1 ]. This paper presents a values reference model (VRM) and an implementation method (IM) for Trustworthiness Including Ethics (TIE) defined based on the VSD rationale mentioned. Also, the piloting of the VRM-TIE and of part of the IM-TIE in a use case involving collaborative robots is presented, addressing both technical and human-related characteristics of the AI systems. The preliminary findings in the work suggest that: (1) AI Trustworthiness is a broad concept that must be analysed in detail, considering the industrial context and other priorities, (2) Achieving a shared understanding among stakeholders is essential but difficult, highlighting the need for a structured dialogue, (3) Adopting this VSD based approach, composed by VRM-TIE and IM-TIE, may have a significant impact on the stakeholders’ minds.

items.title: Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Safety Training for Post-Disaster Responders and Workers: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Post-disaster responders and workers operate in hazardous environments that require rapid decision-making, hazard recognition, and effective safety training. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged in recent years as an innovative tool for immersive occupational safety and health education. This scoping review systematically examines peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of VR for safety training among personnel across a broad range of fields and populations who perform or are trained to perform disaster and emergency response functions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, five electronic databases (PubMed, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and ERIC) were searched, resulting in 2202 identified articles; 19 of which met the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility assessments. The reviewed studies suggest that VR-based safety training, which uses fully immersive simulated environments, can improve learner engagement, situational awareness, hazard recognition, decision-making, and confidence in disaster response scenarios. Several studies have reported higher user satisfaction and increased realism compared with traditional instructional methods such as classroom-based instruction or mock drills. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous, with limitations including small sample sizes, technical challenges, limited scenario diversity, and insufficient long-term evaluation of training outcomes. Overall, VR is a promising supplement to traditional safety and health training for post-disaster responders and workers; however, additional longitudinal research and large-scale studies are needed to further evaluate its effectiveness and long-term applicability in various disaster-response settings.

items.title: Vision-driven retrieval-augmented decision support for plant disease diagnosis using EfficientNetV2 and large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate and timely plant disease diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production and precision farming. However, most existing agricultural decision support systems treat visual disease diagnosis and agronomic recommendation generation as separate processes, either providing image classification results alone or generating recommendations with large language models that are not grounded in domain-specific knowledge. To address this limitation, this study introduces EffiToRag, an end-to-end decision support framework that integrates an EfficientNetV2-based visual diagnosis module with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Rather than relying solely on free-text queries for disease-level retrieval, the proposed approach uses the disease class predicted by EfficientNetV2 as the primary key for retrieving the corresponding record from a structured agronomic knowledge base constructed from peer-reviewed scientific publications and official phytopathological guidelines. The visual diagnosis module was trained using Progressive Training and Class-Aware Tiered Augmentation (CATA) to account for differences in class representation. On a held-out test set comprising 11,621 images across 60 plant health classes, EfficientNetV2-M achieved 99.13% accuracy and a Macro F1 score of 0.9889, with an inference time of 4.39 ms per image on the evaluated GPU. For 500 user queries, the system selected query-relevant knowledge fields with a precision of 0.972 and a recall of 0.985. The factual-consistency assessment combined GPT-4-based evaluation and manual expert review of a random sample of 100 diagnostic reports and yielded a mean factual-consistency score of 0.99. The experts also assigned these reports a mean applicability score of 4.85/5.0. These findings show that visual disease classification, structured agronomic knowledge retrieval, and LLM-based recommendation generation can be integrated within a single decision support pipeline for precision agriculture.

items.title: Vroegdetectie van huidtumoren in het tijdperk van artificiële intelligentie: zijn we er klaar voor?
items.abstract: Early detection of skin tumors in the age of artificial intelligence: are we ready for it? Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly evolving and is increasingly being applied in dermatology, particularly in the early detection of skin tumors. Given the high and increasing incidence of skin cancer and the pressure on specialized care, AI is often proposed as a tool to improve the efficiency of detection and triage. Applications span multiple levels, including risk-based triage on population-level, support for non-dermatologists, and decision support for dermatologists, notably through monitoring of high-risk patients. At the same time, important limitations remain. The performance of AI systems varies significantly depending on the clinical context, image quality, and device used. Smartphone applications used by laypersons for self-assessment of skin-lesion photographs remain insufficiently reliable in real-world conditions, as both image acquisition and diagnostic sensitivity and specificity may be suboptimal. False-positive results may lead to unnecessary anxiety, additional consultations and overdiagnosis, while false-negative results carry clinical risks. There is also a risk that clinicians adopt errors generated by AI systems due to increased trust in the technology. Within the European context, the implementation of AI is further shaped by regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation, the Medical Device Regulation, and the EU AI Act. The AI Act entered into force in 2024 and becomes applicable in phases; for medical AI it may apply alongside the Medical Device Regulation. This highlights that the use of AI entails not only technological, but also clinical and legal responsibility. A critical and stepwise integration of AI into dermatological practice is essential, including clinical validation, user training, and post-deployment performance monitoring. Without adequate understanding of its capabilities and limitations, there is a risk of inefficient and potentially suboptimal care delivery.

items.title: What Does Generalizable AI in Drug Discovery Really Mean?
items.abstract: Abstract Machine learning models increasingly contribute to drug discovery, but their utility depends on performing reliably in their intended deployment setting. Although model generalization is invoked frequently, the drug discovery community lacks a shared vocabulary for how models actually achieve transferability beyond their training data. We argue that achieving generalization requires examining how a model’s inductive bias interacts with its training data to shape the notion of similarity it learns. Without a bias that makes relevant recurring relationships easier to learn as opposed to incidental correlations, models exploit dataset-specific shortcuts. These shortcuts yield high benchmark performance but fail in prospective applications. We therefore propose evaluation principles tailored to a model’s architecture, using diagnostic controls and train−test splits that distinguish transferable learning from the retrieval of familiar training data. This Perspective shows how representational choices shape failure modes across pose-dependent, pose-independent, and foundation model paradigms, and provides a practical framework to help researchers expose shortcuts and interpret predictions.

items.title: What is Hybrid Intelligence? Toward a Multi-Layered Model for Complex Problem-Solving
items.abstract: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

items.title: What Were You Thinking? An LLM-Driven Large-Scale Study of Refactoring Motivations in Open Source Projects
items.abstract: Context . Code refactoring improves software quality without changing external behavior. Despite its advantages, its benefits are hindered by the considerable cost of time, resources, and continuous effort it demands. Aim . Understanding why developers refactor, and which metrics capture these motivations, may support wider and more effective use of refactoring in practice. Method . We performed a large-scale empirical study to analyze developers’ refactoring activity, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify underlying motivations from version control data, comparing our findings with previous motivations reported in the literature. Results . LLMs matched human judgment in 80% of cases, but aligned with literature-based motivations in only 47%. They enriched 22% of motivations with more detailed rationale, often highlighting readability, clarity, and structural improvements. Most motivations were pragmatic, focused on simplification and maintainability. While metrics related to developer experience and code readability ranked highest, their correlation with motivation categories was weak. Conclusions . We conclude that LLMs effectively capture surface-level motivations but struggle with architectural reasoning. Their value lies in providing localized explanations, which, when combined with software metrics, can form hybrid approaches. Such integration offers a promising path toward prioritizing refactoring more systematically and balancing short-term improvements with long-term architectural goals.

items.title: When "brain outsourcing" becomes habit: governmentality dilemmas and learning alienation in agentic workflows
items.abstract: The spread of generative AI has made "brain outsourcing"—delegating cognitive tasks to AI—a common phenomenon in higher education, especially in low-tier private undergraduate colleges. Existing studies explain it mainly at the individual level, neglecting the institutional consequences of the technologies used to govern it. Drawing on design-based research principles, this study conducted a three-group quasi-experiment in a Data Structures course at such a college: an adversarial workflow (Group A, n = 36), a negotiative workflow (Group B, n = 40), and a traditional control group (n = 44), triangulated across five chains of evidence. Results show that Group A's direct-dumping rate fell to 11.1% (vs. 57.5% and 75.0%), yet concealed forms—cosmetic modification and division-of-labor outsourcing—rose compensatorily, leaving the composite outsourcing index unchanged across groups (p = 0.864). Process engagement rose sharply while output authenticity stayed low (comment–code matching 3.62/5; only 27.8% of difficulty tags authentic), indicating "performative engagement". Only 1 of 120 students adopted a self-regulated strategy. In Group A, perceived control rose (+2.17) and negotiation space fell (−0.91) without meaningful growth in autonomy; the 18.3-point advantage over the control group in comprehension depth shrank to 6.8 points in transfer application. The "non-outsourceable" workflow thus changed outsourcing's form, not its deep structure, alienating learning into an adversarial game of evading detection—a new hidden curriculum. Agent design should shift from adversarial surveillance to dialogic support.

items.title: When GenAI helps and when it hurts: testing expertise reversal within a cognitive load framework across different guidance, task complexity, and GenAI access conditions
items.abstract: Abstract Studies have examined the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on students’ learning outcomes, revealing a wide range of effects on performance, cognitive load, and learning processes. However, little is known about whether these effects change with learner expertise and the conditions under which GenAI support is provided. This study examined expertise reversal in GenAI-supported programming education across four eight-week experiments involving Year 3 computer science students from research universities in Saudi Arabia. Drawing on cognitive load theory, the experiments investigated GenAI support, guidance level, task complexity, and access condition in relation to intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, mental effort, and independent programming performance. The findings showed that GenAI support produced greater reductions in extraneous load and stronger independent performance among lower-expertise learners, while higher-expertise learners retained smaller benefits. Detailed guidance produced a crossover expertise reversal, benefiting lower-expertise learners while increasing extraneous load and weakening performance among higher-expertise learners. Higher task complexity increased cognitive demands and reduced performance across expertise levels, with greater effects among lower-expertise learners. Personalised access also benefited lower-expertise learners more strongly without disadvantaging higher-expertise learners. Overall, the findings distinguish a crossover expertise reversal under detailed GenAI guidance from diminishing benefits as learner expertise increases under other support and access conditions. The effects of task complexity further demonstrate that expertise-dependent differences do not necessarily constitute a reversal in instructional effectiveness. We recommend that effective GenAI support requires careful calibration to learners’ existing knowledge and the cognitive demands of learning.

items.title: When Trust Does the Thinking: A Pre-Specified Test of Mindsponge Theory's Prediction That Content Counts Less as Trust Rises
items.abstract: Mindsponge theory (MT) holds that the mind evaluates incoming information most thoroughly when it neither trusts nor distrusts the source, and least at either extreme. Its testing program states this as prediction P2: the weight that content carries in acceptance follows an inverted U across trust. Rival accounts expect the weight to stay constant (Bayesian combination) or to rise with trust (monotone moderation). We report the first admitted test of P2, on the open Human-AI Interactions dataset of Vodrahalli et al. (2022). In that study, 207 US adults judged the art period of 32 paintings, received advice described as 65% or 95% accurate (identical advice in both groups), and gave a final answer. Because participants were about 66 to 70% accurate on their own, the 65% source sits near indifference and the 95% source is highly trusted, so the design covers the trusted half of the curve, where MT predicts that content weight falls. The rule, fixed and fingerprinted before any final answer was read, measured how strongly a participant’s own first judgment of the advised label governed whether the final answer sided with the advice. The weight was 4.42 logits at 65% and 3.43 at 95%; the difference was 0.99 (SE 0.34, z = 2.94, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.65), and the verdict is supported. Adding a 65/80/95 comparison gives 4.43, 3.68 and 3.45. The result survives two-way clustering and alternative codings. A post-verdict decomposition shows that trust mattered only when people’s own judgment opposed the advice; within those trials the drop in weight is clearer on a continuous measure (z = 2.17) than on the pre-specified binary one (z = 0.64). Because trials in which participants already agreed with the advice cannot show acceptance, these disagreement trials are the cleaner test of P2. The result clearly disfavors monotone moderation, disfavors constant Bayesian weighting with moderate rather than strong evidence, and does not separate MT from simple opinion averaging. It supports the trusted half of P2, not the full inverted U.

items.title: Who chose the label? Voluntary versus mandated AI disclosure in tourism marketing
items.abstract: Generative AI is being used extensively by destination marketing organisations (DMOs) to create promotional imagery, and new regulation requires disclosure of some synthetic content. Previous research indicates that revealing an AI source can reduce perceived authenticity but treats disclosure as a single cue. This study investigated whether travellers react differently when the AI label is presented as the DMO's own decision or as a legally mandated requirement. A simulated single factor, three condition (no label, voluntary label, mandated label) between-subjects online experiment with N = 387 adult participants. The analysis was based on the Persuasion Knowledge Model and attribution theory, using ANCOVA, bootstrapped parallel mediation analyses (multicategorical predictor), moderation by attitudes towards AI and robustness checks. Both labels reduced perceived authenticity compared to no label (voluntary: d = −0.59; mandated: d = −0.74). The voluntary label raised perceived DMO integrity (d = 0.38), producing a positive indirect effect on visit intention. The mandated label earned no integrity credit, and its negative indirect effect through authenticity was not compensated. These effects were not significantly moderated by general attitudes toward AI. The study distinguishes between what the AI label says and who is seen to have chosen it, thereby furthering the research on persuasion-knowledge in tourism and providing a model that DMOs can test for disclosure in the regulatory era.

items.title: Who Gets the Credit? Generative AI Contribution Disclosure and Performance Appraisal Fairness among Faculty Members in Indian Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by knowledge workers to prepare reports, teaching materials, research summaries, presentations and administrative documents. Although such tools may improve speed and output quality, they create a human resource management question that is not resolved by measuring productivity alone: how should an employee receive performance credit when a work product is created through a combination of human judgement and AI assistance? This conceptual paper develops a research framework to examine the relationship between GenAI contribution disclosure, perceived ownership of work, procedural fairness in performance appraisal and employees’ trust in institutional HR practices among faculty members in Indian higher education institutions. It proposes that transparent disclosure of the type and extent of AI assistance may improve appraisal fairness when institutions use clear contribution criteria and retain human review. However, disclosure may also create a perceived competence penalty if AI-assisted work is interpreted as evidence of lower individual capability. The paper proposes a quantitative, multi-source research design involving faculty members and their academic supervisors. It does not report empirical findings; the hypotheses and framework are intended for subsequent field testing. The study seeks to extend HRM research by connecting human–AI contribution attribution with faculty performance management in the Indian higher education context.

items.title: Who Punishes LLM Alignment? User Characteristics and the Evaluation of Ethical Response Refusals
items.abstract: Ethical refusals are essential for aligning large language models (LLMs) with safety constraints, yet users often penalize them in comparative evaluations. Whether this refusal penalty varies systematically across users remains unclear. Drawing on human–computer interaction research, we examine how users’ evaluative priorities and usage intensity shape responses to ethical refusals. Using the PRISM alignment dataset, which links LLM evaluations to user characteristics, we find that safety preferences significantly mitigate refusal penalties, whereas preferences for helpfulness, fluency, and creativity do not. Heavy users penalize refusals more strongly, an association substantially mediated by lower safety preferences. These findings suggest that acceptance of safety-aligned behavior depends primarily on users’ safety orientation rather than preferences for instrumental response qualities. Our results highlight the limitations of evaluating LLM safety alignment through aggregate user preferences and underscore the importance of accounting for user heterogeneity in evaluation benchmarks and deployment decisions.

items.title: WHY AI IS AN ADAPTIVE LEADERSHIP AND ADULT DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGE
items.abstract: Abstract Organizations continue investing trillions of dollars in artificial intelligence (AI), yet many fail to realize meaningful business value. This article argues that the primary barrier to successful AI transformation is not the technology itself, but a widespread leadership misconception termed the AI Readiness Illusion: the belief that organizations become AI‐ready when their technology is ready. Drawing on adaptive leadership, organizational change, adult development theory, and leadership development research, the article reframes AI transformation as a human development challenge rather than a technology implementation challenge. Integrating Heifetz's work on adaptive leadership, Beer and Nohria's Theory E and Theory O framework, Kegan's theory of adult development, and empirical research on leadership development, the article introduces the concept of human readiness as an organization's capacity to think, learn, adapt, and exercise professional judgment as technology evolves. It argues that technical training alone cannot prepare employees for the complexity AI introduces into decision‐making and organizational life. Instead, leaders must cultivate environments characterized by shared vision, compassion, relational energy, coaching, and continuous learning to develop the judgment, critical thinking, and adaptability required for sustained transformation. The article concludes that organizations will realize greater value from AI by investing in human readiness alongside technological capability.

items.title: Wisdom-Based Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is forcing education to confront a question that long predates AI: What is education ultimately for? Modern educational systems have become highly effective at transmitting knowledge, developing analytical capacity, and preparing young people for further education and employment. These are important achievements. Yet they represent only part of what education can do for a human being. When education is organized primarily around knowledge acquisition, competition, assessment, and selection, the development of the person as a whole can become secondary. The emergence of artificial intelligence makes this limitation increasingly visible. Machines can already store, retrieve, synthesize, and process information at a scale no human being can or should attempt to match. If education continues to define human development primarily in terms of information processing and analytical performance, it risks preparing young people to compete with machines in domains in which machines will increasingly excel. I propose a different direction: Wisdom-Based Education. Wisdom-Based Education places the cultivation of the whole human being alongside intellectual development as a fundamental purpose of education. Drawing upon Ren Xue, a contemporary system of human development rooted in Chinese wisdom traditions, it views the human being as an integrated totality of Body, Qi, and Jingshen (composite of consciousness, heart and True Self) and proposes that education should deliberately cultivate self-awareness, inner stability, health, ethical discernment, compassion, creativity, wisdom, and the capacity to contribute meaningfully to others. Its central hypothesis is that wisdom is not merely the accidental product of age or experience. Capacities associated with wisdom can be intentionally cultivated. This proposition changes what we teach, how we teach, how teachers understand their role, how parents participate in education, how children learn from relationships, and how we define educational success. Academic learning remains essential, but it becomes part of a larger developmental process directed toward five broad outcomes: health, happiness, wellbeing, continuing growth, and meaningful contribution. This paper presents the philosophical foundations of Wisdom-Based Education, its model of human development, its implications for educational practice, and a pathway through which its propositions can be translated into curricula, pilot programs, teacher and parent preparation, and systematic research. Its fundamental claim is simple: the next transformation of education must be concerned not merely with what human beings know, but with what human beings can become.

items.title: Working with GenAI: how a human-centered mindset and GenAI understanding drive employee autonomy and competence
items.abstract: Purpose Research has paid limited attention to why employees differ in maintaining autonomy and competence in GenAI-enabled workplaces and how individual resources translate into these outcomes. Addressing this gap, this research examines how human-centered mindset and GenAI understanding influence autonomy and competence through perceived instrumentality of work relationships and helping behavior. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 339 employees. Covariance-based structural equation modeling via Analysis of Moment Structures tested the hypothesized relationships among six latent constructs. A marker variable procedure assessed common method bias. Findings Human-centered mindset and GenAI understanding are associated with autonomy and competence through different social mechanisms. Perceived instrumentality of work relationships emerged as the more consistent pathway, while helping behavior operated selectively for GenAI understanding. These findings highlight the distinct roles of value-based orientations and knowledge-based resources in psychological need satisfaction in GenAI-enabled workplaces. Originality/value This research extends Self-Determination Theory into GenAI-enabled workplaces by identifying human-centered mindset and GenAI understanding as antecedents of psychological need satisfaction. It distinguishes value-based orientations from knowledge-based resources and introduces perceived instrumentality of work relationships as a relational-cognitive mechanism that sustains autonomy and competence in human-AI collaborative work environments.

items.title: Working With Robots: How Robot Proportion in Human-Robot Teams and Robot Anthropomorphism Shape Employee Turnover Intention
items.abstract: Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human-robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a three-wave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human-robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human-robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

items.title: YR-MPE: a modular desktop platform for agent-operable and reproducible phylogenetic workflows
items.abstract: Abstract Phylogenomic analyses combine many tools, file formats and execution modes. Desktop graphical user interfaces make individual steps accessible but hide their state from scripts; command-line pipelines make steps scriptable but leave parameter discovery, provenance and recovery to the user; and emerging LLM agents can call command-line tools but cannot inspect a GUI session or its artifacts. We present YR-MPE, a modular desktop platform whose YPhylo Workbench unifies these modes through a typed workspace, a plugin contract and a semantic action layer. Every operation in the action registry is exposed as a machine-callable action; controls without a CLI equivalent are declared GUI-only. The workspace records every imported plugin result as a run with its inputs, parameters, tool identity and output artifacts, the latter with SHA-256 hashes; each compiled workflow step becomes its own run. A placeholder compiler turns JSONL command sequences into reproducible workflow DAGs, while a skill layer maps each declared control to the corresponding command-line option; plugins with tool-specific contracts expose tool-specific actions. YR-MPE runs natively on Windows and bundles alignment, model selection, maximum-likelihood, Bayesian and species-tree inference, molecular dating, selection and visualization tools. We describe the interface and its provenance/workflow substrate, and report three representative recipes: an organelle-genome workflow, a single-locus model-to-tree analysis, and an agent-driven run. YR-MPE is released under GPL-3.0 at https://github.com/Gipsy-The-Sheller/YR-MPE.

items.title: “The System Says So”: Making Sense of AI-Driven HRM, Conditional Trust and Employee Well-Being in Saudi Arabian Organisations
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose This study explores how employees in Saudi Arabian organisations perceive artificial intelligence (AI)-driven human resource management (HRM) and how their interpretations of the technology shape trust in HR systems and employee well-being. Design/methodology/approach: This qualitative study draws on 35 semi-structured interviews analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings: Employees’ perceptions of AI-driven HRM were shaped by transparency, human involvement, and contextual sensitivity. Employees expressed conditional trust in AI used for administrative tasks, but were more reluctant to trust it with consequential decisions such as performance appraisals. Concerns about dignity, autonomy, and mental well-being were closely linked to perceptions of AI-driven HRM as context-blind and overly reductive. Originality/value: By placing employee sensemaking at the centre of the analysis, this study clarifies how AI-driven HRM is interpreted in organisational settings and how such interpretations shape trust and well-being. Practical implications: The study highlights the need for a hybrid HRM model that combines technological efficiency with transparency, contextual awareness, and meaningful human oversight.

items.title: A consumer neuroscience approach to examining how augmented reality and QR codes support product and brand sustainability communication in retail settings
items.abstract: This research explores the use of Augmented Reality (AR) and Quick Response (QR) codes as tools for communicating sustainability-related information in a quasi-realistic retail setting. It combines neurophysiological and self-report measures to investigate how these technologies influence consumers’ sustainability perceptions, emotional engagement, and cognitive workload. Participants took part in a simulated shopping experience, where they were exposed to one of three experimental conditions: traditional packaging, smartphone-mediated QR code scanning, and smartphone-mediated Augmented Reality exploration of coffee packaging. Cognitive workload (measured via electroencephalography) and emotional engagement (measured via skin conductance and heart rate) were recorded alongside self-report measures of green company orientation (GCO), green product informativeness (GPI), and brand familiarity. Findings indicate that while both AR and QR codes evoke more positive emotions and lead to higher perceptions of GCO and GPI, AR usage is also associated with higher cognitive workload. Additionally, brand familiarity enhanced self-report scores but not neurophysiological ones, without interacting with the interaction modality. This research provides a multi-level (implicit neurophysiological and explicit self-reported) perspective on the impact of digital packaging formats on sustainability communication. The findings contribute to ongoing discussions on how interactive technologies can support effective communication, implicit emotions, and consumer engagement with sustainability in retail environments.

items.title: A Fuzzy Bayesian Network for Berthing Risk Analysis of Ultralarge Vessels
items.abstract: Abstract With the increasing growth of port trade throughput, ultralarge vessel (ULV) berthing safety has become a critical operational link in ensuring the safety of life and property while improving port efficiency. This study proposes an approach that integrates fuzzy logic with a rule-based Bayesian network (RBN) within the traditional failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) to provide berthing risk analysis for ULVs. Using the FMEA method, ULV’s berthing risk is characterized from three perspectives—occurrence, severity, and detection—and expert judgments obtained from questionnaires are fuzzified through fuzzy logic reasoning. An RBN model is developed to infer posterior risk distributions and to output the expected risk value and risk entropy value, which measure risk magnitude and uncertainty, respectively. The results indicate that human-related factors, particularly fatigue, communication errors, and insufficient experience, exhibit the highest expected risk values with low entropy, identifying them as priority targets for intervention. Vessel-related factors show moderate-to-high levels with notable coupling effects with human factors, while tugboat-related factors present lower expected values but higher uncertainty, indicating strong scenario dependence. This study offers both theoretical support for uncertainty-aware maritime risk assessment and practical guidance for optimizing crew management, communication strategies, and berthing operations under complex conditions.

items.title: A human-centred framework for AI integration in the curriculum
items.abstract: This paper reports ongoing work at La Trobe University to cultivate a shared understanding of effective artificial intelligence (AI) integration through the design of a human-centred framework for embedding AI literacies into teaching and learning. In response to conceptual ambiguity of AI curriculum integration, the Online Education Design team developed an operational definition positioning AI as infrastructure for active learning and the educator as the central decision-maker in the learning design process. This definition was translated into the AI-Informed Learning Design Framework, a four-step process, in which educators define the learning goal, select an AI pedagogical role, apply an AI Assessment Scale boundary check, then design learning activities that develop disciplinary knowledge and AI literacy. Supported by a four-level scaffolding model governing students' growing independence in AI use, the framework was piloted through two rounds, using a design-based research methodology. Feedback from Round one highlighted opportunities to refine the framework whilst also emphasising broader sector-wide tensions surrounding AI integration, including educators’ reluctance to use AI and concerns about the framing of some AI roles in teaching and learning. Early findings from the second round suggest improved educator engagement and a stronger understanding of the framework.
